summary: Every player secretly checks or swaps roles in a brief night phase, then the whole table argues, bluffs, and accuses for a few loud minutes before a single simultaneous vote decides the outcome. It plays in about ten minutes but generates disproportionate table talk and replay value because roles differ every round and nobody, including former werewolves, is ever fully sure who anyone is.
praised: Extremely fast setup and playtime, easy to fire off multiple rounds in a row
Strong social deduction and bluffing even with no elimination and no moderator needed once you use the app
High replayability since the role mix changes what strategies matter each game
Great as a party icebreaker with large, mixed-experience groups
The companion app narrator removes the need for a dedicated moderator
criticised: Very light strategically, almost entirely social rather than mechanical
Some special roles have little to do or feel weaker than others (e.g., Villager, Insomniac in certain mixes)
Can be chaotic or overwhelming for shy players or large tables all talking over each other
Outcome can hinge heavily on who is more convincing rather than any decision quality
Needs a confident 'loud' player or app to keep discussion moving, or it stalls

interaction.kind: open accusation, bluffing, and group argument

scoring.why: The village wins by lynching at least one werewolf (or werewolves win if none are lynched, with a few role-specific exceptions like the Tanner), decided purely by the single end-of-round vote.
